books.title: The Garden Party and Other Stories
books.author: Katherine Mansfield
books.desc: Fifteen stories of everyday moments, from a family's summer by the sea in New Zealand to a garden party shadowed by a neighbour's death.
about: In the title story, the wealthy Sheridan family prepare to give a garden party. Young Laura supervises the workmen putting up the marquee, while her mother has ordered masses of lilies. Then the news arrives that Mr Scott, a working-class neighbour, has been killed just outside their gate. Laura wants the party called off, but her mother and her sister Jose do not agree. The collection opens with "At the Bay", a portrait of a family's summer days in a seaside settlement, and also includes "The Daughters of the Late Colonel", "Life of Ma Parker", "Miss Brill" and "Her First Ball".
Mansfield's stories capture fleeting moments of feeling and perception, class differences, loneliness and the discovery of death, in a concise, poetic and modern style.

"The Garden Party" first appeared in the Westminster Gazette in February 1922, and the collection The Garden Party and Other Stories was published the same year. Several stories, including "At the Bay" and "The Garden Party", were written in Switzerland, and the title story draws on Mansfield's childhood home in Wellington.
books.author_short: New Zealand short-story writer (1888–1923), an important figure of literary modernism, author of Bliss and The Garden Party.
author_long: Kathleen Mansfield Beauchamp was born on 14 October 1888 in Wellington, New Zealand, into a prominent family; her father later became chairman of the Bank of New Zealand. She settled in Europe and married the critic John Middleton Murry. Diagnosed with tuberculosis in 1917, she died in France on 9 January 1923, aged 34.
Her collections include Bliss (1920) and The Garden Party and Other Stories (1922).

books.title: This Side of Paradise
books.author: F. Scott Fitzgerald
books.desc: A handsome, self-absorbed young Midwesterner goes to Princeton convinced he has a great destiny, and searches for it through love, war and disillusion.
about: Amory Blaine, raised by his eccentric mother Beatrice, believes that he is destined for greatness without knowing what form it will take. At Princeton he dabbles in literature, makes friends such as the idealistic Burne Holiday and the poet Tom D'Invilliers, and falls in and out of love with a series of young women, among them Isabelle, the debutante Rosalind and the wild Eleanor, while his mentor Monsignor Darcy advises him from afar.
Fitzgerald's first novel portrays the manners, ambitions and romances of a privileged younger generation in the 1910s, and the search of a young man for identity and meaning.

This Side of Paradise was published by Charles Scribner's Sons in March 1920, when Fitzgerald was 23. Its title comes from Rupert Brooke's poem "Tiare Tahiti". It caused a sensation and made its author a spokesman for rebellious youth.

books.title: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
books.author: James Joyce
books.desc: From early childhood to university, young Stephen Dedalus rebels against family, Church and nation to become an artist.
about: The novel follows Stephen Dedalus from his first memories, through his years at the Jesuit boarding school of Clongowes Wood and the family's decline into poverty, a violent quarrel over Irish politics at a Christmas dinner, adolescent guilt and a period of intense religious devotion, to his years as a student in Dublin, where he debates art and beauty with his friends Cranly, Davin and Lynch and decides to leave Ireland.

Joyce's first novel, a Künstlerroman written in a modernist style, uses a language that changes as its hero grows up, and makes extensive use of free indirect speech to follow Stephen's developing consciousness. It explores religion, Irish nationalism, family and the vocation of the artist.

Joyce reworked an earlier abandoned novel, Stephen Hero, into this five-chapter book. Thanks to Ezra Pound it was serialised in the London magazine The Egoist in 1914 and 1915, and it was published as a book in 1916 by B. W. Huebsch in New York.

books.title: The Diary of a Nobody
books.author: George and Weedon Grossmith
books.desc: Charles Pooter, a London clerk with an exaggerated sense of his own importance, records the small humiliations of his daily life.
about: Charles Pooter, a clerk in the City firm of Perkupp's, has just moved with his wife Carrie into "The Laurels", Brickfield Terrace, Holloway. In his diary he records the events of the following fifteen months: visits from his friends Gowing and Cummings, quarrels with tradesmen, social evenings that end in embarrassment, and the troubles caused by his son Lupin, who wants to make his own way in the world and becomes engaged to Daisy Mutlar.

The humour of the book comes from Pooter's unconscious pomposity and from the way his sense of importance is constantly punctured by gaffes and minor social disasters, in a gentle satire of lower-middle-class respectability.
The Diary first appeared as an intermittent serial in Punch in 1888 and 1889, and was published as a book, with additional text and illustrations by Weedon Grossmith, in 1892.
books.author_short: English brothers George Grossmith (1847–1912), comedian and Gilbert and Sullivan star, and Weedon Grossmith (1854–1919), actor and illustrator, co-authors of The Diary of a Nobody.
author_long: George Grossmith was born in Islington, London, on 9 December 1847 and died on 1 March 1912. A comedian, singer and composer, he created nine roles in the comic operas of Gilbert and Sullivan between 1877 and 1889, and was famous for his own comic piano sketches.

His younger brother Walter Weedon Grossmith, born on 9 June 1854 and died on 14 June 1919, was an actor, painter and playwright. Together they wrote The Diary of a Nobody (1892), which Weedon illustrated.

books.title: Salomé
books.author: Oscar Wilde
books.desc: At the court of Herod, the princess Salomé becomes obsessed with the imprisoned prophet Jokanaan and demands his head as the price of her dance.
about: On a moonlit night, on a terrace of the palace of Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Judaea, the young Syrian captain and the page of Herodias watch the princess Salomé. From a cistern rises the voice of the prophet Jokanaan (John the Baptist), whom Herod keeps prisoner. Salomé, Herodias's daughter and Herod's stepdaughter, insists on seeing him and is fascinated by him, but he rejects her. Herod, who desires Salomé, begs her to dance for him, promising her anything she asks.
Wilde's one-act tragedy turns the biblical story into a Symbolist drama of desire, obsession and death, written in a rhythmic, incantatory language full of repeated images, above all the moon.

Wilde wrote Salomé in French in Paris in late 1891. Rehearsals with Sarah Bernhardt in London in 1892 were stopped when the Lord Chamberlain refused a licence. The French text was published in 1893 and an English translation in 1894; the English text here comes from a 1907 edition with drawings by Aubrey Beardsley. The first performance was given in Paris on 11 February 1896 by the Théâtre de l'Œuvre, while Wilde was in prison. This edition offers the French original and the English translation credited to Lord Alfred Douglas.
